evidence.snippet: Here we present evidence that mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-1 (FGFR1) gene, which maps to 8p, cause one form of familial Pfeiffer syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The primary report identifying FGFR1 as a Pfeiffer locus, which is the causative relationship this record asserts.

evidence.snippet: A C to G transversion in exon 5, predicting a proline to arginine substitution in the putative extracellular domain, was identified in all affected members of five unrelated PS families but not in any unaffected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Gives the recurrent allele and its segregation: present in every affected family member and in no unaffected individual across five families.

evidence.snippet: A specific, rare mutation p.Pro252Arg, located between the second and third extracellular immunoglobulin-like domain of FGFR1, is associated with mild clinical signs.
evidence.explanation: Sources the p.Pro252Arg codon number, its position in the protein, and its association with mild clinical signs.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal disorders caused by type 1 mutations include Pfeiffer syndrome (PS) and osteoglophonic dysplasia
evidence.explanation: Confirms FGFR1 (type 1) mutations as a cause of Pfeiffer syndrome.

genes/0.notes: FGFR1 is the minority Pfeiffer locus and the recurrent p.Pro252Arg allele it carries is associated with mild clinical signs, while FGFR2 accounts for the majority of cases. Neither the clinical severity types nor the gene-defined forms is a relabelling of the other, and no source found supports a one-to-one mapping between them: an FGFR2 variant is reported in a patient classified as the mild type 1, and a hospital series describes severe FGFR2-associated disease, so FGFR2 spans the severity range. The two axes are therefore curated as overlapping has_subtypes rows rather than as a mapping. The Europe PMC queries behind that were TITLE:"Pfeiffer syndrome" AND (FGFR2 OR FGFR1); ABSTRACT:"Pfeiffer" AND ABSTRACT:"FGFR1" AND ABSTRACT:"FGFR2" AND (ABSTRACT:"severe" OR ABSTRACT:"mild"); and "Pfeiffer syndrome" AND FGFR1 AND "type 1" AND ABSTRACT:FGFR2. ClinGen's own grade for the FGFR1-Pfeiffer relationship is not stated here: the repository's committed ClinGen caches carry the FGFR2 assertion only, and the gene-validity CSV those caches are built from is not part of the repository.

evidence.snippet: FGFR2 | HGNC:3689 | Pfeiffer syndrome | MONDO:0007043 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the FGFR2-Pfeiffer syndrome gene-disease relationship as definitive with autosomal dominant inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Here we report a second locus for PS on chromosome 10q25, and present evidence that mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-2 (FGFR2) gene on 10q25 cause PS in an additional subset of familial and sporadic cases.
evidence.explanation: Establishes FGFR2 on 10q25 as the second Pfeiffer locus, alongside FGFR1 on chromosome 8 — the genetic heterogeneity this entry now covers in full.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, this T to C change is identical to a mutation in FGFR2 previously reported in Crouzon syndrome, a phenotypically similar disorder but one lacking the hand and foot anomalies seen in PS.
evidence.explanation: Records that an identical FGFR2 allele is reported in both Pfeiffer and Crouzon syndrome, so genotype alone does not separate them — the digital features do.

treatments/0.description: Surgical expansion of the cranial vault to relieve intracranial pressure and correct skull deformity. May require staged procedures depending on severity.

evidence.snippet: It was determined on institutional review that his vision loss was attributed to the tightness of the bicoronal flap due to scarring from past Le Fort III procedures in combination with permissive hypotension and anemia.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the proposed mechanism of a severe visual complication of repeated midface advancement in Pfeiffer syndrome.

evidence.snippet: This case demonstrates the only documented episode of bilateral posterior ischemic optic neuropathy in a pediatric patient and describes a rarely documented risk factor.
evidence.explanation: Records that this is a single documented case, so no frequency claim is made.

treatments/1.description: Le Fort III or monobloc osteotomy to advance the midface, improving airway, proptosis, and facial appearance. Repeat midface surgery is common in FGFR-related syndromic craniosynostosis, and the scarring left by earlier procedures is itself a risk factor: the first reported paediatric case of bilateral posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy after craniofacial surgery occurred in a 13-year-old with Pfeiffer syndrome undergoing Le Fort II advancement, attributed to bicoronal flap tightness from prior Le Fort III surgery combined with permissive hypotension and anaemia. This is a single case and does not establish a rate, but it identifies a mechanism — cumulative operative scarring plus intraoperative hypoperfusion — specific to the repeatedly operated syndromic craniosynostosis patient.

evidence.snippet: Urinary concentrations of BPA and several phthalate metabolites were significantly associated with increased risk of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the exposure-disease association in a longitudinally sampled pregnancy cohort, which is what makes phthalates an environmental factor for this entry.

evidence.snippet: an interquartile range increase of urinary concentrations of BPA (1.53; 95% CI: 1.04, 2.25) and MEP (monoethyl phthalate) (1.72; 95% CI: 1.28, 2.30) at 10 weeks gestation was associated with onset of preeclampsia
evidence.explanation: Reports the BPA hazard ratio for preeclampsia onset with an early-gestation exposure window, which is the whole basis for listing BPA here.

evidence.snippet: Pregnant rats were exposed to PS-MP, which induced PE-like symptoms including elevated blood pressure, increased proteinuria, and altered expression of angiogenic factors.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the exposure produces the maternal syndrome in an animal model, which is the only outcome evidence this entry has.

evidence.snippet: Highly expressed PSG2 in PE placentas contributes to PE pathogenesis by activating the TGF-β/Smad3 pathway, thereby inhibiting EMT and MMPs expression and attenuating trophoblast proliferation, migration, and invasion.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PSG2 upregulation in preeclamptic placentas as a mechanism activating TGF-β/Smad3 signaling.

steps/3.description: Placenta-derived pregnancy-specific beta-1-glycoprotein 2 (PSG2) is upregulated in preeclamptic placentas and activates the TGF-β/Smad3 signaling pathway in extravillous trophoblasts. This placental-derived mechanism cell-autonomously suppresses trophoblast epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and downregulates matrix metalloproteinases (MMP2/MMP9), thereby reducing trophoblast proliferation, migration, and invasion capacity. This is distinct from the sEng-mediated inhibition of endothelial TGF-beta signaling modeled downstream in the maternal circulation.

evidence.snippet: We have found that the combination of maternal KIR AA genotype with a fetal HLA-C2 is associated with an increased risk of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Supports the KIR/HLA-C maternal-fetal genotype interaction as an upstream risk mechanism.

evidence.snippet: too much inhibition of uNK cells leading to poor trophoblast invasion into the uterine arteries.
evidence.explanation: Supports the proposed bridge from excessive inhibitory uterine NK signaling to poor trophoblast invasion.

evidence.snippet: Decidual NK (dNK) cells significantly contribute to the vascular remodeling through the secretion of cytokines and angiogenic mediators in normal placental development.
evidence.explanation: Review evidence supports the role of decidual NK cells in normal placental vascular remodeling.

evidence.snippet: Activation of KIR2DS1+ dNK by HLA-C2 stimulated production of soluble products including GM-CSF, detected by intracellular FACS and ELISA. We demonstrated that GM-CSF enhanced migration of primary trophoblast and JEG-3 trophoblast cells in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the soluble mediator this node was previously missing. The protective arm of the KIR/HLA-C system works through GM-CSF secreted by activated decidual NK cells, which enhances trophoblast migration; a KIR AA genotype lacking the activating receptor cannot produce that signal.

evidence.snippet: we have demonstrated that trophoblast expresses both paternally and maternally inherited HLA-C surface proteins and that maternal KIR AA frequencies are increased in affected pregnancies only when the fetus has more group 2 HLA-C genes (C2) than the mother
evidence.explanation: Sharpens the genotype combination this node describes. The risk is not carried by maternal KIR AA with any fetal C2, but specifically by a fetal C2 dose exceeding the mother's, which points to a paternally inherited allogeneic effect rather than a shared maternal-fetal genotype.

steps/4.description: Decidual natural killer cells normally interact with fetal extravillous trophoblast HLA-C through maternal KIR receptors and help regulate placental development, trophoblast invasion, and spiral artery remodeling. In susceptible maternal-fetal genotype combinations, especially maternal KIR AA with fetal HLA-C2, excessive inhibitory signaling can reduce dNK activation and impair trophoblast invasion. This upstream immune maladaptation is modeled as an early-onset, placenta-dominant trigger rather than as the established antiangiogenic effector pathway itself.

evidence.snippet: Risk factors for the disease include maternal comorbidities, such as chronic kidney disease, hypertension and obesity
evidence.explanation: Identifies maternal vascular, renal, and metabolic comorbidities that can reduce endothelial reserve.

steps/5.description: Late-onset preeclampsia can be modeled as a threshold phenomenon in which near-term fetal and placental demands interact with maternal cardiovascular, renal, metabolic, or inflammatory susceptibility. In this model, placental antiangiogenic stress can be less severe than in early-onset disease, but maternal endothelial reserve is lower, so hypertension and end-organ dysfunction emerge when physiologic demand exceeds vascular supply.

evidence.snippet: PE is initiated by poor placentation due to inadequate trophoblast invasion and improper spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental hypoxia.
evidence.explanation: Directly describes the defective trophoblast invasion and spiral artery remodeling as the initiating event in preeclampsia.

evidence.snippet: a growing body of evidence suggests that products of an ischemic or a stressed placenta are responsible for the vascular changes that characterize this syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Supports the concept that placental ischemia (from defective remodeling) drives vascular pathology.

steps/6.description: In normal pregnancy, extravillous trophoblasts invade the uterine decidua and remodel maternal spiral arteries into high-capacitance, low-resistance vessels. In preeclampsia, this invasion is shallow and incomplete, resulting in narrow, high-resistance spiral arteries that fail to adequately perfuse the placenta. The resulting placental ischemia and hypoxia trigger downstream pathological cascades.

evidence.snippet: Sustained HIF-1α activation drives mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, amplifying placental injury.
evidence.explanation: Supports the mitochondrial and oxidative-stress content of this node as a consequence of sustained HIF-1alpha activity.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset preeclampsia is a severe placental disorder driven primarily by impaired uteroplacental perfusion and early placental ischemia.
evidence.explanation: Scopes this hypoxic-signaling node to early-onset disease, matching the subtype restriction of the hypothesis it belongs to.

steps/7.description: Tightly controlled hypoxia guides normal trophoblast differentiation and vascular remodeling in early gestation. When hypoxia becomes persistent or excessive, hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1alpha) is stabilized rather than degraded, and sustained HIF-1alpha activity becomes the transcriptional link between placental ischemia and the antiangiogenic shift: it drives mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress that amplify placental injury, and it promotes antiangiogenic transcriptional programs including sFlt-1 upregulation. This node is curated from review-level synthesis; no HIF-1alpha perturbation experiment has been performed in human placental tissue, so the edge to antiangiogenic factor release is mechanistically motivated rather than directly demonstrated in humans. It is distinct from the HIF-1alpha/TFRC ferroptosis axis modelled under microplastic exposure, which is a rodent finding about a specific exposure rather than the endogenous ischemic response described here.

evidence.snippet: we confirm that placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt1), an antagonist of VEGF and placental growth factor (PlGF), is upregulated in preeclampsia, leading to increased systemic levels of sFlt1 that fall after delivery.
evidence.explanation: Landmark paper demonstrating that placental sFlt-1 is upregulated in preeclampsia with systemic elevation.

evidence.snippet: The sFlt-1 level increased beginning approximately five weeks before the onset of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Shows that sFlt-1 rises weeks before clinical disease, consistent with placental release preceding symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Increased levels of sFlt-1 and reduced levels of PlGF predict the subsequent development of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the predictive anti-angiogenic imbalance pattern.

evidence.snippet: sEng inhibits formation of capillary tubes in vitro
evidence.explanation: In vitro evidence that soluble endoglin has anti-angiogenic effects.

evidence.snippet: Its effects in pregnant rats are amplified by coadministration of sFlt1, leading to severe preeclampsia including the HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome and restriction of fetal growth.
evidence.explanation: Rat model demonstrates that sEng synergizes with sFlt-1 to produce severe preeclampsia including HELLP syndrome.

evidence.snippet: This triggers the release of anti-angiogenic factors such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng), causing widespread endothelial dysfunction and systemic inflammation.
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the anti-angiogenic cascade from placental hypoxia to endothelial dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Key findings in early-onset preeclampsia included disrupted syncytiotrophoblast and extravillous trophoblast angiogenic signaling, characterized by an up-regulation of FLT1 and down-regulation of PGF, consistent with an angiogenic imbalance.
evidence.explanation: Locates the antiangiogenic shift in the specific placental cell types this node names, rather than inferring it from circulating protein levels. The other evidence here measures sFlt-1 and PlGF in maternal blood; this is the transcriptional counterpart in syncytiotrophoblast and extravillous trophoblast.

steps/8.description: The ischemic placenta releases excess anti-angiogenic factors, primarily soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng), into the maternal circulation. sFlt-1 acts as a decoy receptor that sequesters VEGF and PlGF, while sEng inhibits TGF-beta signaling. Together, these factors create a systemic anti-angiogenic state that disrupts normal endothelial function. Levels of sFlt-1 rise and PlGF fall weeks before clinical onset.

evidence.snippet: This review synthesizes the most recent data on NLRs in PE, focusing on their role in disease genesis, pathogenic processes, biomarker potential, and therapeutic consequences.
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive review documenting NLRP3 inflammasome role in preeclampsia genesis and pathogenesis.

steps/9.description: Dysregulated NOD-like receptor (NLR) signaling, particularly NLRP3 inflammasome activation, contributes to placental and systemic inflammation in preeclampsia. Placental stress from ischemia and poor trophoblast invasion triggers pattern recognition receptors that activate the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (NLRP3, ASC, and pro-caspase-1). Active caspase-1 processes pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms, driving excessive IL-1β and IL-18 release from placental macrophages, trophoblasts, and maternal immune cells. This inflammasome-mediated inflammatory cascade amplifies oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and systemic inflammation, contributing to hypertension and multi-organ involvement in preeclampsia.

evidence.snippet: In addition to endothelial dysfunction, increasing attention has focused on the role of thromboinflammation and immunothrombosis in the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia. Immunothrombosis refers to the bidirectional interaction between immune and coagulation pathways whereby inflammatory activation promotes thrombosis and thrombotic processes amplify inflammation.
evidence.explanation: Defines immunothrombosis as the bidirectional interaction between immune and coagulation pathways in preeclampsia.

evidence.snippet: Cytokines stimulate tissue factor expression on endothelial cells and monocytes, while simultaneously promoting platelet activation and impairing fibrinolysis.
evidence.explanation: The tissue factor induction and fibrinolysis suppression this node is named for, quoted from the sentence that states both.

steps/10.description: Systemic pro-inflammatory cytokines from placental ischemia and NLRP3 inflammasome activation (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17, IFN-γ) stimulate tissue factor expression on endothelial cells and monocytes, triggering the extrinsic coagulation cascade. Impaired anticoagulant pathways (reduced protein C, antithrombin) and suppression of fibrinolysis (elevated plasminogen activator inhibitor-1) hold the resulting thrombin generation and fibrin deposition unopposed. This is the initiating limb of immunothrombosis - the bidirectional interaction in which inflammatory activation promotes thrombosis and thrombotic processes amplify inflammation. Conformance to the thrombogenesis module is supported here because the cited review describes an explicit tissue factor to thrombin to fibrin branch rather than the TTP-type microangiopathy the module's scope note excludes.

evidence.snippet: Emerging evidence also highlights the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and extracellular vesicles in the propagation of immunothrombosis. NETs provide a structural scaffold that enhances platelet aggregation and fibrin deposition, while extracellular vesicles carry tissue factor and inflammatory cytokines, amplifying both coagulation and endothelial damage at distant vascular sites
evidence.explanation: Documents how NETs and extracellular vesicles amplify the immunothrombotic cascade.

steps/11.description: Activated platelets release pro-inflammatory mediators that amplify endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment. Neutrophil extracellular traps provide a structural scaffold that enhances platelet aggregation and fibrin deposition, while circulating extracellular vesicles carry tissue factor and inflammatory cytokines to distant vascular sites. Together these make the process self-perpetuating rather than self-limiting, which is what distinguishes immunothrombosis from ordinary hemostasis.

evidence.snippet: administration of sFlt1 to pregnant rats induces hypertension, proteinuria, and glomerular endotheliosis, the classic lesion of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that sFlt-1 causes the clinical triad of hypertension, proteinuria, and glomerular endotheliosis.

evidence.snippet: Maternal endothelial dysfunction due to circulating factors of fetal origin from the placenta is a hallmark of pre-eclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Identifies endothelial dysfunction from placental factors as the hallmark of preeclampsia.

evidence.snippet: sEng impairs binding of TGF-beta1 to its receptors and downstream signaling including effects on activation of eNOS and vasodilation, suggesting that sEng leads to dysregulated TGF-beta signaling in the vasculature.
evidence.explanation: Biochemical/cell-based evidence that sEng disrupts TGF-beta receptor binding and eNOS activation.

steps/12.description: The anti-angiogenic imbalance causes widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction, manifesting as vasoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and activation of the coagulation cascade. This leads to the clinical features of hypertension, proteinuria (from glomerular endotheliosis), hepatic dysfunction, cerebral edema, and thrombocytopenia. The characteristic renal lesion is glomerular endotheliosis.

evidence.snippet: administration of sFlt1 to pregnant rats induces hypertension, proteinuria, and glomerular endotheliosis, the classic lesion of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the renal lesion and proteinuria after sFlt-1 exposure in pregnant rats.

steps/13.description: Antiangiogenic injury to glomerular endothelial cells disrupts the fenestrated filtration barrier, producing glomerular endotheliosis and proteinuria. This renal branch is the most direct organ-specific consequence of the sFlt-1/VEGF/PlGF imbalance.

evidence.snippet: Cerebrovascular dysfunction during preeclampsia can lead to cerebral edema, seizures, stroke, and potentially maternal mortality.
evidence.explanation: Directly links preeclampsia cerebrovascular dysfunction to acute neurologic complications.

evidence.snippet: PRES can be caused by an acute elevation in blood pressure that overcomes cerebral artery and arteriole vasoconstriction, resulting in a loss of CBF autoregulation, disruption to the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and vasogenic edema formation
evidence.explanation: Supports the autoregulatory failure, BBB disruption, and vasogenic edema mechanism for eclampsia/PRES-like manifestations.

steps/14.description: Cerebral vascular dysfunction in preeclampsia can include impaired autoregulatory reserve, endothelial injury, blood-brain barrier disruption, and vasogenic edema. This branch connects systemic endothelial dysfunction to headache, visual symptoms, PRES-like edema, seizures, stroke, and eclampsia.

evidence.snippet: These alterations create a prothrombotic state characterized by microvascular thrombosis, endothelial injury, and organ ischemia.
evidence.explanation: The microvascular thrombosis and organ ischemia this node is named for, quoted from the sentence that states both.

steps/15.description: Microthrombi form in the microvasculature of critical maternal organs (kidney, liver, brain, placenta), reducing perfusion and exacerbating endothelial injury. This is the point at which the prothrombotic state becomes organ injury, and it is the node from which the severe maternal complications of preeclampsia follow.

evidence.snippet: The dysfunctional placenta in women developing HELLP initiates a cascade of events that eventually results in liver dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: Places HELLP liver injury downstream of placental dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The latter causes ischemic damage and progressive demise of hepatocytes.
evidence.explanation: Supports ischemic hepatocyte injury downstream of sinusoidal obstruction.

steps/16.description: In severe preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome, systemic endothelial injury and inflammatory prothrombotic signaling can be amplified in hepatic sinusoids, where low shear favors microthrombi and fibrin deposition. Sinusoidal obstruction causes ischemic hepatocyte injury, elevated liver enzymes, platelet consumption, and microangiopathic hemolysis.

evidence.snippet: The disease presents with new-onset hypertension and often proteinuria in the mother, which can progress to multi-organ dysfunction, including hepatic, renal and cerebral disease, if the fetus and placenta are not delivered.
evidence.explanation: Identifies proteinuria as a frequent but not universal feature of preeclampsia.

steps/17.description: New-onset proteinuria, typically >=300 mg per 24-hour urine collection or protein/creatinine ratio >=0.3 mg/dL. While historically required for diagnosis, current guidelines recognize preeclampsia can occur without proteinuria if other signs of end-organ dysfunction are present.

evidence.snippet: This disease represents a spectrum of hypertensive disease in pregnancy, beginning with gestational hypertension and progressing to develop severe features, ultimately leading to its more severe manifestations, such as eclampsia and HELLP syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Human clinical anchor placing HELLP syndrome — of which thrombocytopenia is a defining component — on the preeclampsia spectrum.

evidence.snippet: leading to severe preeclampsia including the HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome
evidence.explanation: Rat sFlt1/sEng co-administration model reproduces the low-platelet component of HELLP. Model-organism support for the mechanism only; it is not the primary evidence for the human phenotype.

steps/18.description: Low platelet count, particularly prominent in HELLP syndrome. Reflects endothelial activation and consumptive coagulopathy.

evidence.snippet: once thought to be a disease of the central nervous system, recognized by the occurrence of seizures (ie, eclampsia)
evidence.explanation: Eclamptic seizures are the historically defining severe complication of preeclampsia.

steps/19.description: New-onset tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with preeclampsia, defining the transition to eclampsia. Represents a severe neurological complication that can occur antepartum, intrapartum, or postpartum.

evidence.snippet: Severe preeclampsia is defined as blood pressure (BP) >160/110 mmHg with warning signs such as headache, blurring of vision, and epigastric pain.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly identifies headache as a warning sign of severe preeclampsia.

steps/20.description: Severe, persistent headache that is a warning sign for severe preeclampsia and eclampsia, indicating cerebral involvement.

evidence.snippet: Severe preeclampsia is defined as blood pressure (BP) >160/110 mmHg with warning signs such as headache, blurring of vision, and epigastric pain.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly identifies blurring of vision as a warning sign of severe preeclampsia.

steps/21.description: Blurred vision and other visual disturbances are warning signs of severe preeclampsia, reflecting cerebral edema and vasospasm.

evidence.snippet: This disease represents a spectrum of hypertensive disease in pregnancy, beginning with gestational hypertension and progressing to develop severe features, ultimately leading to its more severe manifestations, such as eclampsia and HELLP syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Human clinical anchor placing HELLP — whose "H" is microangiopathic hemolysis — within the preeclampsia spectrum.

evidence.snippet: leading to severe preeclampsia including the HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome
evidence.explanation: Rat model reproduces the hemolysis component of HELLP; model-organism corroboration rather than primary human evidence.

steps/22.description: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia as part of HELLP syndrome, reflecting erythrocyte destruction in damaged microvasculature.

evidence.snippet: Overall, the conclusion is that the interaction between maternal KIR on uNK cells and fetal HLA class I molecules on trophoblast has a physiological function in regulating the development of the placenta
evidence.explanation: Places maternal KIR and fetal trophoblast HLA interactions upstream of placental development.

edges/0.description: Dysregulated dNK-KIR recognition of fetal trophoblast HLA-C can bias the decidua toward inadequate trophoblast invasion and poor spiral artery transformation.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset preeclampsia has many features in common with atherosclerosis, whereas late-onset preeclampsia seems to result from a mismatch of fetal demands and maternal supply, that is, a metabolic crisis.
evidence.explanation: Supports linking late-onset disease to a maternal demand-supply threshold model.

edges/1.description: Maternal vascular, renal, and metabolic comorbidities lower the threshold for systemic endothelial dysfunction as late-pregnancy demand rises.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, PSG2 activated the TGF-β/Smad3 signaling pathway, and the TGFBR1 inhibitor SB431542 effectively reversed PSG2-mediated inhibition of EMT, MMP2/MMP9 expression, and trophoblast functional impairment.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates PSG2-TGF-β/Smad3 activation suppresses EMT and MMPs, impairing trophoblast function.

edges/2.description: PSG2-activated TGF-β/Smad3 signaling suppresses epithelial-mesenchymal transition and metalloproteinase expression, reducing trophoblast invasiveness and contributing to defective spiral artery remodeling.

evidence.snippet: PE is initiated by poor placentation due to inadequate trophoblast invasion and improper spiral artery remodeling, leading to placental hypoxia. This triggers the release of anti-angiogenic factors such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin (sEng), causing widespread endothelial dysfunction and systemic inflammation.
evidence.explanation: Directly describes the causal chain from defective trophoblast invasion through placental hypoxia to anti-angiogenic factor release.

edges/3.description: Placental ischemia from poor spiral artery remodeling triggers release of anti-angiogenic factors into the maternal circulation.

evidence.snippet: Persistent or excessive hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1α, leading to defective trophoblast invasion, impaired spiral artery remodeling, and progressive placental ischemia.
evidence.explanation: Places HIF-1alpha stabilization downstream of the sustained hypoxia produced by impaired spiral artery remodeling.

edges/4.description: Persistent hypoxia from a high-resistance, poorly remodeled uteroplacental circulation stabilizes HIF-1alpha in the placenta.

evidence.snippet: Key characteristics of PE include dysregulated NLR activity, excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and impaired trophoblast invasion.
evidence.explanation: Links impaired trophoblast invasion and dysregulated NLR (NLRP3) activity as co-occurring core features of preeclampsia, supporting placental invasion failure upstream of inflammasome activation.

edges/5.description: Placental ischemia and stress arising from defective trophoblast invasion and poor spiral artery remodeling activate pattern recognition receptors and the NLRP3 inflammasome in placental and decidual immune cells.

evidence.snippet: At the transcriptional level, HIF-1α promotes antiangiogenic programs, including sFlt-1 upregulation, resulting in systemic angiogenic imbalance and maternal endothelial dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: States the transcriptional step from stabilized HIF-1alpha to sFlt-1 overproduction and systemic angiogenic imbalance that this edge represents.

edges/6.description: Sustained HIF-1alpha activity promotes antiangiogenic transcriptional programs, including sFlt-1 upregulation, converting placental ischemia into a systemic angiogenic imbalance.

evidence.snippet: increased circulating sFlt1 in patients with preeclampsia is associated with decreased circulating levels of free VEGF and PlGF
evidence.explanation: Human clinical observation showing sFlt-1 elevation associates with decreased free VEGF and PlGF.

evidence.snippet: resulting in endothelial dysfunction in vitro that can be rescued by exogenous VEGF and PlGF.
evidence.explanation: In vitro demonstration that endothelial dysfunction from sFlt-1 excess is reversible with VEGF/PlGF.

edges/7.description: Anti-angiogenic factors in the maternal circulation cause widespread endothelial injury and dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: Recent studies underscore the important contribution of NOD-like receptors (NLRs), particularly the NLRP3 inflammasome, to PE development.
evidence.explanation: Directly establishes NLRP3 inflammasome as a key contributor to preeclampsia development.

evidence.snippet: Key characteristics of PE include dysregulated NLR activity, excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and impaired trophoblast invasion.
evidence.explanation: Links dysregulated NLRs to excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction—the hallmarks of preeclampsia pathophysiology.

edges/8.description: NLRP3-derived inflammatory mediators (IL-1β, IL-18) amplify endothelial activation and dysfunction, synergizing with anti-angiogenic factors to produce systemic inflammation and vascular injury.

evidence.snippet: The cytokine surge characteristic of pre‐eclampsia—primarily involving TNF‐α, IL‐6, and IL‐1β—induces the expression of tissue factor on endothelial cells and circulating monocytes.
evidence.explanation: Names IL-1beta among the cytokines that induce tissue factor expression, placing inflammasome-derived cytokine output upstream of coagulation activation.

edges/9.description: NLRP3-derived cytokines (IL-1beta, IL-18) join the wider TNF-alpha/IL-6 surge that induces tissue factor on endothelial cells and monocytes, initiating the extrinsic coagulation cascade and establishing the immunothrombotic state.

evidence.snippet: Cytokines stimulate tissue factor expression on endothelial cells and monocytes, while simultaneously promoting platelet activation and impairing fibrinolysis. This phenomenon, referred to as immunothrombosis, represents a convergence of immune and coagulation mechanisms, where the body's attempt to contain inflammation paradoxically causes microvascular thrombi and vascular obstruction.
evidence.explanation: States that the same cytokine signal drives tissue factor expression and platelet activation, which is the edge asserted here.

edges/10.description: The same cytokine signal that induces tissue factor promotes platelet activation, and the thrombin generated by the cascade is itself a platelet agonist, so cascade activation and platelet activation propagate together.

evidence.snippet: NETs provide a structural scaffold that enhances platelet aggregation and fibrin deposition, while extracellular vesicles carry tissue factor and inflammatory cytokines, amplifying both coagulation and endothelial damage at distant vascular sites
evidence.explanation: Describes the platelet-plus-fibrin thrombus this edge carries into the microvascular occlusion node.

edges/11.description: Platelet aggregation on a NET scaffold, with fibrin deposition, produces the microthrombi that occlude the maternal microvasculature.

evidence.snippet: These alterations create a prothrombotic state characterized by microvascular thrombosis, endothelial injury, and organ ischemia. The concept of immunothrombosis provides an important mechanistic framework for understanding how inflammatory and coagulation pathways converge to drive disease progression and contribute to complications such as HELLP syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, placental infarction, and adverse fetal outcomes
evidence.explanation: Links immunothrombosis directly to HELLP syndrome pathogenesis via microvascular thrombosis and organ ischemia.

edges/12.description: Immunothrombotic microvascular injury with hepatic sinusoidal microthrombi and fibrin deposition causes hepatocyte ischemia and the HELLP phenotype (hemolysis from mechanical destruction of red blood cells by fibrin strands).

evidence.snippet: microthrombi reduce perfusion, exacerbate endothelial injury, and contribute to the development of severe complications such as HELLP syndrome, eclampsia, and multi-organ dysfunction
evidence.explanation: The quote states that microthrombi contribute to HELLP syndrome, of which thrombocytopenia is a defining component. It does not describe platelet consumption; this review's only mention of thrombocytopenia is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia as an LMWH risk, so no consumptive mechanism is claimed here.

edges/13.description: Microvascular thrombosis contributes to HELLP syndrome, of which thrombocytopenia is a defining feature. The intermediate omitted here is the HELLP node itself, which carries its own platelet-consumption account.

evidence.snippet: administration of sFlt1 to pregnant rats induces hypertension, proteinuria, and glomerular endotheliosis, the classic lesion of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Directly links sFlt-1-driven endothelial dysfunction to the renal lesion and proteinuria.

edges/14.description: Systemic antiangiogenic endothelial injury targets glomerular capillaries, producing endotheliosis and proteinuria.

evidence.snippet: Particularly in microcirculations with extremely low shear forces, such as in the hepatic sinusoids, this will facilitate microthrombi formation and fibrin deposition eventually resulting in obstruction of the sinusoids similar as in SOS.
evidence.explanation: Supports the liver-specific endothelial microvascular mechanism for HELLP-related hepatic injury.

edges/15.description: Endothelial injury and prothrombotic inflammation can cause hepatic sinusoidal microthrombi, fibrin deposition, hepatocyte ischemia, and the HELLP phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Cerebrovascular dysfunction during preeclampsia can lead to cerebral edema, seizures, stroke, and potentially maternal mortality.
evidence.explanation: Supports a CNS-specific downstream branch from endothelial/cerebrovascular dysfunction to eclampsia-related complications.

edges/16.description: Cerebral endothelial dysfunction and impaired vascular autoregulation can disrupt the blood-brain barrier, produce vasogenic edema or PRES, and precipitate eclamptic seizures.

edges/17.description: Glomerular endothelial swelling and filtration-barrier injury increase urinary protein loss.

edges/18.description: Prothrombotic endothelial injury consumes platelets in the HELLP microangiopathy.

edges/19.description: Microangiopathic vascular injury fragments erythrocytes and produces hemolysis.

edges/20.description: Cerebral edema and vascular dysfunction can precipitate eclamptic seizures.

edges/21.description: Cerebrovascular dysfunction contributes to severe headache in preeclampsia with severe features.

edges/22.description: PRES-like posterior cerebral involvement can produce visual symptoms.

evidence.snippet: We found consistent associations between DEHP metabolites and preeclampsia across pregnancy, with a potential heightened risk associated with concentrations later in pregnancy.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the exposure-outcome relationship across gestation. PARTIAL because it establishes risk of the syndrome without evidence for the placental step this edge points at.

evidence.snippet: significant associations between mono-n-butyl phthalate (MBP) and higher MMP1 by 7.86 % (95 % CI: 0.49, 15.76) and between mono oxononyl phthalate (MONP) and higher MMP2 by 8.30 % (95 % CI: 2.22, 14.75)
evidence.explanation: Supplies the candidate mediator - phthalate exposure altering the matrix metalloproteinases that remodel spiral arteries. PARTIAL because this cohort measured circulating biomarkers, not preeclampsia or placental MMP expression, so the mediation is inferred rather than shown. The direction is also unresolved and is the most informative thing about this citation: the reported association is with *higher* MMP1 and MMP2, whereas this entry models defective trophoblast invasion as MMP2/MMP9 *suppression* (the PSG2 node). Whether a systemic rise in circulating metalloproteinases is compatible with local suppression at the invading trophoblast front is not addressed by either source.

edges/23.description: Drawn to the placental node because that is where preeclampsia risk is thought to be set, not because any step was demonstrated. The cited hazard ratios are for onset of the syndrome; nothing between exposure and trophoblast behaviour was measured. The intermediates are marked unknown deliberately - the matrix metalloproteinase finding below is the leading candidate, not an established link, and it points the opposite way from the MMP2/MMP9 suppression this file models as the invasion defect.

evidence.snippet: oxidized di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) metabolites were associated with decreases in PlGF as well as increases in the sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio
evidence.explanation: Measures the node's own output - PlGF and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio - against exposure, which is what makes this edge land on a mechanism rather than on the diagnosis.

edges/24.description: The better-supported of the two phthalate edges, because here the outcome measured is this node itself rather than the syndrome. In the same birth cohort, oxidised DEHP metabolites tracked with falling placental growth factor and a rising sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio across gestation - the exact angiogenic imbalance this node describes. What remains unknown is the step between the plasticiser and the trophoblast that secretes these factors, so the intermediates stay marked unknown.

evidence.snippet: BPA, however, was associated with increased sFlt-1 as well as the sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio in both crude and adjusted models.
evidence.explanation: Associates BPA exposure with the anti-angiogenic shift this node names, which is the mechanism-level claim the hazard-ratio paper cannot make.

edges/25.description: BPA tracked with higher circulating sFlt-1 and a higher sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio across gestation in the same cohort that produced its preeclampsia hazard ratio, which puts the exposure and this node in the same population rather than in two unrelated studies. It is still an association between a urinary exposure biomarker and a plasma factor, with no placental step measured.

evidence.snippet: PS-MP triggered ferroptosis in placental trophoblast cells by activating the HIF-1α/TFRC axis, resulting in iron overload and oxidative stress
evidence.explanation: Names the intermediate steps that make this an indirect edge with known mechanism rather than an unexplained association.

evidence.snippet: PS-MP exposure impaired trophoblast migration, invasion, and angiogenesis; these effects were ameliorated by ferroptosis inhibition
evidence.explanation: The rescue arm: blocking the proposed intermediate restores the trophoblast behaviour this node describes, tying the exposure to the node causally within the model.

edges/26.description: The rodent chain runs from particle exposure through HIF-1alpha/TFRC activation to iron overload, oxidative stress and trophoblast ferroptosis, and lands on impaired trophoblast migration, invasion and angiogenesis - this node's content. Ferroptosis inhibition rescues those defects, which is what makes the intermediates known rather than assumed. The species and dose gap to human exposure is unaddressed.

evidence.snippet: We report the first GWAS of offspring from preeclamptic pregnancies and discovery of the first genome-wide significant susceptibility locus (rs4769613; P = 5.4 × 10-11) in 4,380 cases and 310,238 controls.
evidence.explanation: Replaces a general statement that FLT1 polymorphisms matter with the actual genome-wide significant locus, its effect size context, and the fact that it was found in offspring rather than mothers.

evidence.snippet: This locus is near the FLT1 gene encoding Fms-like tyrosine kinase 1, providing biological support, as a placental isoform of this protein (sFlt-1) is implicated in the pathology of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Ties the genome-wide significant signal to the placental sFlt-1 isoform this entry models as the effector.

evidence.snippet: Genetic and epigenetic modifications, including polymorphisms in the Fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (FLT1) gene and altered microRNA (miRNA) expression, play critical roles.
evidence.explanation: Identifies FLT1 polymorphisms as playing a critical role in preeclampsia.

evidence.snippet: we confirm that placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt1), an antagonist of VEGF and placental growth factor (PlGF), is upregulated in preeclampsia
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates sFlt-1 (FLT1 gene product) upregulation in preeclamptic placentas.

genes/0.notes: Encodes fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (VEGFR1). Alternative splicing produces the soluble isoform sFlt-1, which is overexpressed by the preeclamptic placenta and acts as a decoy receptor sequestering VEGF and PlGF. Polymorphisms in FLT1 are associated with preeclampsia susceptibility. The risk variant is carried in the fetal rather than the maternal genome, which is the strongest genetic argument that placental sFlt-1 overproduction is causal rather than reactive. Note the association reported for that locus was strongest in late-gestation preeclampsia with normally grown offspring, so it is evidence for the antiangiogenic axis in preeclampsia generally and not specifically for the early-onset subtype.

evidence.snippet: Increased levels of sFlt-1 and reduced levels of PlGF predict the subsequent development of preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: PlGF reduction is a key predictive feature of preeclampsia.

genes/1.notes: Encodes placental growth factor (PlGF), a VEGF family member essential for placental angiogenesis. Free PlGF levels are reduced in preeclampsia due to sequestration by excess sFlt-1, and low PlGF is an early biomarker.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that sEng may act in concert with sFlt1 to induce severe preeclampsia.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the pathogenic role of soluble endoglin (ENG gene product) in severe preeclampsia.

genes/2.notes: Encodes endoglin, a TGF-beta coreceptor. The soluble form (sEng) is elevated in preeclampsia and synergizes with sFlt-1 to induce severe disease including HELLP syndrome in animal models.

evidence.snippet: increased circulating sFlt1 in patients with preeclampsia is associated with decreased circulating levels of free VEGF and PlGF
evidence.explanation: Human clinical data showing that sFlt-1 excess sequesters free VEGF in preeclampsia patients.

evidence.snippet: resulting in endothelial dysfunction in vitro that can be rescued by exogenous VEGF and PlGF.
evidence.explanation: In vitro evidence that exogenous VEGF can rescue sFlt-1-induced endothelial dysfunction.

genes/3.notes: Encodes vascular endothelial growth factor A, a key mediator of angiogenesis and endothelial homeostasis. Sequestration of free VEGF by excess sFlt-1 in preeclampsia contributes to endothelial dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: which can progress to multi-organ dysfunction, including hepatic, renal and cerebral disease, if the fetus and placenta are not delivered.
evidence.explanation: Identifies delivery as the necessary intervention to prevent progression.

treatments/0.description: Delivery of the fetus and placenta is the only definitive treatment for preeclampsia. Timing depends on gestational age and severity, balancing maternal risk against fetal prematurity. Generally recommended at 37 weeks for preeclampsia without severe features, and earlier if severe features or maternal/fetal deterioration occurs.

evidence.snippet: Preterm preeclampsia occurred in 13 participants (1.6%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 35 (4.3%) in the placebo group (odds ratio in the aspirin group, 0.38; 95% confidence interval, 0.20 to 0.74; P=0.004).
evidence.explanation: The ASPRE trial demonstrated a 62% reduction in preterm preeclampsia with aspirin 150 mg daily.

evidence.snippet: In women with a history of vasculo-placental disease, low dose of aspirin (Strong recommendation, Quality of the evidence moderate) at a dosage of 100-160mg per day (Weak recommendation, Quality of the evidence low)
evidence.explanation: The French College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists clinical practice guidelines make a Strong recommendation for low-dose aspirin in women with a history of vasculo-placental disease; the specific 100-160 mg per day dosage is graded only a Weak recommendation.

treatments/1.description: Low-dose aspirin (150 mg daily) initiated at 11-14 weeks of gestation in women identified as high risk reduces the incidence of preterm preeclampsia by approximately 62%. This is a preventive intervention, not a treatment for established disease.

evidence.snippet: Its primary mechanism involves irreversible inhibition of platelet cyclooxygenase‐1, leading to reduced thromboxane A2 production and a shift toward a vasodilatory and antithrombotic state.
evidence.explanation: Names the platelet target that makes this an inhibitory edge onto the platelet-activation node rather than onto the coagulation cascade.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Irreversible inhibition of platelet cyclooxygenase-1 reduces thromboxane A2 production, which is the platelet-activation limb of immunothrombosis. This is prophylaxis rather than treatment of established disease, so the edge describes what aspirin acts on, not a reversal of established thrombosis.

evidence.snippet: Women allocated magnesium sulphate had a 58% lower risk of eclampsia (95% CI 40-71) than those allocated placebo (40, 0.8%, vs 96, 1.9%; 11 fewer women with eclampsia per 1000 women).
evidence.explanation: The Magpie trial demonstrated that magnesium sulfate halves eclampsia risk.

treatments/2.description: Magnesium sulfate is the first-line agent for prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures. It halves the risk of eclampsia in women with preeclampsia and probably reduces maternal mortality.

evidence.snippet: Nifedipine (C17H18N2O6), labetalol (C19H24N2O3), and hydralazine (C8H8N4) are commonly used drugs, and all are recommended as first-line agents.
evidence.explanation: Identifies labetalol as a recommended first-line agent for acute hypertensive management in pregnancy.

treatments/3.description: Labetalol is a first-line antihypertensive for acute blood pressure management in severe preeclampsia, used to prevent hypertensive emergencies and stroke.

evidence.snippet: oral nifedipine has been proposed as a first-line alternative to intravenous labetalol.
evidence.explanation: Identifies nifedipine as a first-line alternative antihypertensive for severe preeclampsia.

treatments/4.description: Nifedipine is an alternative first-line oral antihypertensive for acute severe hypertension in preeclampsia.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset preeclampsia has many features in common with atherosclerosis, whereas late-onset preeclampsia seems to result from a mismatch of fetal demands and maternal supply, that is, a metabolic crisis.
evidence.explanation: Supports modeling early-onset preeclampsia separately from late-onset disease.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, late-onset preeclampsia exhibited comparatively subtle transcriptional changes, suggestive of a distinct pathophysiological process driven by maternal cardiovascular maladaptation, placental aging, cellular senescence and oxidative stress.
evidence.explanation: Supports restricting this model to early-onset disease on transcriptomic rather than clinical grounds. The comparison is made within one placental single-cell atlas, so the early-onset and late-onset profiles were measured on the same platform.

evidence.snippet: The association was strongest in offspring from pregnancies in which preeclampsia developed during late gestation and offspring birth weights exceeded the tenth centile.
evidence.explanation: Argues against treating fetal FLT1 genetics as support for an early-onset-specific model. The locus is the strongest genetic evidence that the antiangiogenic axis is causal in preeclampsia at all, but its own stratification points to late-gestation disease with normal fetal growth, which is the presentation this hypothesis explicitly does not claim.

hypotheses/0.description: In early-onset preeclampsia, immune maladaptation at the maternal-fetal interface and defective trophoblast invasion produce severe placental malperfusion before clinical disease. Placental hypoxia and stress drive a marked antiangiogenic shift, especially excess sFlt-1 and soluble endoglin with reduced free PlGF, causing maternal endothelial dysfunction and organ-specific renal, hepatic, CNS, and uteroplacental manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset preeclampsia has many features in common with atherosclerosis, whereas late-onset preeclampsia seems to result from a mismatch of fetal demands and maternal supply, that is, a metabolic crisis.
evidence.explanation: Supports a late-onset model centered on maternal-fetal demand-supply mismatch.

hypotheses/1.description: In late-onset preeclampsia, placental stress and antiangiogenic imbalance can be milder, while maternal cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, or immune susceptibility lowers the threshold for systemic endothelial dysfunction as fetal and placental demands peak near term. This model explains cases with limited placental lesions but clinically important hypertension and end-organ dysfunction.

open_questions/0.rationale: The antiangiogenic endothelial dysfunction pathway is comparatively well supported, but the initiating biology is heterogeneous. Resolving whether early-onset and late-onset preeclampsia are dominated by distinct upstream triggers would improve subtype-specific biomarker interpretation, preventive trial design, and organ-risk prediction.

evidence.snippet: Cell culture and animal studies have demonstrated potential reproductive toxicity of these particles; however, their association with adverse fertility or pregnancy outcomes in humans is not known.
evidence.explanation: A systematic review stating the human outcome evidence is absent, which is precisely the mismatch this discussion records.

evidence.snippet: These findings identified PS-MP-induced ferroptosis as a critical mechanism underlying placental dysfunction, highlighting PS-MP as a potential environmental risk factor for PE.
evidence.explanation: The model-side claim, stated by its authors as potential rather than established, which is the half of the picture that does exist.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every element of the microplastic-preeclampsia claim except the human endpoint is in place. Plastic particles are demonstrably present in human placental tissue; a rodent model reproduces the maternal syndrome and names an interventionally supported trophoblast mechanism. What no study has done is relate measured placental or maternal plastic burden to preeclampsia in people, and a 2024 systematic review found the human outcome literature essentially empty. The exposure is therefore modelled here with an explicit species caveat rather than as an established contributor. Note the two entries for plastic-derived chemistry in this file sit on opposite footings: the phthalate and bisphenol A entries have human risk estimates but no mechanism, while this one has a mechanism but no human endpoint. Neither gap is filled by the other.

evidence.snippet: Dextran sulfate apheresis lowered circulating sFlt-1, reduced proteinuria, and stabilized blood pressure without apparent adverse events to mother and fetus.
evidence.explanation: The positive half of the interventional argument, in which the analyte fell and the syndrome improved together.

evidence.snippet: This pilot study supports the hypothesis that extracorporeal apheresis can lower circulating sFlt-1 in very preterm preeclampsia. Further studies are warranted to determine whether this intervention safely and effectively prolongs pregnancy and improves maternal and fetal outcomes in this setting.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own scoping of what an uncontrolled series of eight women establishes, which is that sFlt-1 can be lowered and not yet that lowering it prolongs pregnancy.

evidence.snippet: Although H.E.L.P.-apheresis induced a transient peak baseline levels did not change and rather stabilized sFlt-1 levels at pre-apheresis levels throughout treatments, with sFlt-1/PLGF ratio remaining unaffected.
evidence.explanation: Dissociates the clinical benefit of apheresis from sFlt-1 removal. This study prolonged pregnancy while leaving the analyte and the ratio unchanged, which is why it cannot be counted as interventional support for the antiangiogenic mechanism.

evidence.snippet: However, without changing sFlt-1 levels below baseline lowering lipids or other yet undefined factors appear to be of more relevance than reducing sFlt-1.
evidence.explanation: The authors' explicit alternative attribution, naming lipid lowering or unidentified factors ahead of sFlt-1 reduction.

evidence.snippet: Finally, as the removal of circulating sFlt-1 (soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase receptor-1) from pre-eclamptic patients significantly improves the clinical outcome, it fulfils the Hill's experiment principle
evidence.explanation: The review-level claim that the reversibility criterion is already satisfied. It is included because it is the position this gap qualifies: the criterion is asserted at review level on the strength of the pilot series alone.

open_questions/2.rationale: Interventional reversibility is the strongest argument that sFlt-1 excess is causal rather than reactive, and it is the argument this entry's canonical hypothesis leans on hardest. The evidence for it is thinner than it is usually presented. One pilot series of eight women showed that dextran sulfate cellulose apheresis lowers sFlt-1 dose-dependently, reduces proteinuria, stabilises blood pressure, and prolongs pregnancy by 15 to 23 days, but it is uncontrolled and its own authors call for further studies. The second apheresis study, using heparin-mediated extracorporeal LDL precipitation, prolonged pregnancy against historic controls yet did not lower sFlt-1 below baseline and left the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio unaffected, so its authors concluded that lipid lowering or undefined factors mattered more than sFlt-1 reduction. Read together, the two studies establish that apheresis helps and leave open whether sFlt-1 removal is why. No Phase III trial of a targeted sFlt-1 reduction has been completed. This matters for the entry because it sets how much causal weight the antiangiogenic node can carry, and because a therapy chosen on the strength of the wrong mechanism would be optimised against the wrong endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Retrieved results consistently reported C4, C3, and factor H reduction, and increased circulating levels of C4d, Bb, factor D, C3a, C5a, and C5b-9 in PE compared to normal pregnancies, depicting an overall scenario of excessive C activation and aberrant C regulation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that complement activation is a consistent finding in preeclampsia across 41 studies, which is what makes the independence question worth asking rather than dismissing.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, we also discussed emerging pitfalls in C analysis, mainly due to a lack of experimental uniformity and biased cohort selection among different studies and laboratories
evidence.explanation: The same review's caveat on its own evidence base, which is why the complement signal is recorded here as an open question rather than as a curated mechanism node.

evidence.snippet: We describe a patient presenting with severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome at 26 weeks gestation that was treated with Eculizumab, a targeted inhibitor of complement protein C5, which resulted in marked clinical improvement and complete normalization of lab parameters.
evidence.explanation: The whole of the interventional evidence, which is one patient. No angiogenic factors were measured, so the case cannot separate a complement effect from an antiangiogenic one.

evidence.snippet: Successful use of Eculizumab in this case suggests that complement inhibition may be an effective treatment strategy for severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own hedged conclusion, which claims a possible treatment strategy and not an independent pathway.

open_questions/3.rationale: This entry models HELLP as a liver-specific amplification of the systemic endothelial injury caused by the antiangiogenic shift, and the canonical hypothesis claims HELLP among the subtypes it explains. Complement is the main candidate for a branch that would sit outside that account. The activation itself is not in doubt: a systematic review of 41 studies reports consistent consumption of C3, C4 and factor H alongside raised C4d, Bb, factor D, C3a, C5a and C5b-9 in preeclampsia. What is unresolved is dependence. The only interventional evidence is a single case in which C5 inhibition normalised laboratory parameters and prolonged pregnancy by 17 days, and that report measured no angiogenic factors at all, so it cannot show that the benefit was independent of sFlt-1. Resolving this decides whether complement inhibition belongs alongside or instead of antiangiogenic approaches in HELLP, and whether this entry needs a separate complement branch rather than a note.

evidence.snippet: Glycosylation of STT3A- and STT3B-specific acceptors is decreased in fibroblasts carrying the corresponding mutated gene and expression of the STT3A (p.Val626Ala) allele in STT3A-deficient HeLa cells does not rescue glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: The recessive allele fails to complement STT3A loss in cells.

steps/1.description: Homozygous missense variants in STT3A reduce the function of the OST-A catalytic subunit. The recurrent p.Val626Ala allele does not restore glycosylation when expressed in STT3A-deficient cells.

evidence.snippet: Modeling of the variants in the 3D structure of the OST complex indicated that all variants are located in the catalytic site of STT3A, suggesting a direct mechanistic link to the transfer of oligosaccharides onto nascent glycoproteins.
evidence.explanation: Structural modeling places every dominant variant in the catalytic site.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, expression of STT3A at mRNA and steady-state protein level in fibroblasts was normal, while glycosylation was abnormal.
evidence.explanation: Normal protein amount with abnormal glycosylation argues against simple haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: In S. cerevisiae, expression of STT3 containing variants homologous to those in affected individuals induced defective glycosylation of carboxypeptidase Y in a wild-type yeast strain and expression of the same mutants in the STT3 hypomorphic stt3-7 yeast strain worsened the already observed glycosylation defect.
evidence.explanation: Homologous mutants impair glycosylation despite wild-type STT3, the signature of a dominant-negative effect.

evidence.snippet: Variants clustered in conserved catalytic regions, with recurrent p.Arg405 across de novo, inherited, and mosaic cases supporting a mutational hotspot and likely dominant-negative mechanism.
evidence.explanation: Pooled-cohort review concluding a likely dominant-negative mechanism.

steps/2.description: Heterozygous missense variants cluster in the catalytic site of STT3A, including residues such as Arg405 that stabilize the dolichol-pyrophosphate donor during transfer. STT3A mRNA and protein levels are normal in patient fibroblasts, yet glycosylation is abnormal, and homologous yeast STT3 mutants impair glycosylation even in the presence of wild-type STT3. The mutant subunit is therefore thought to poison the complex rather than simply halve its amount. That inference rests on the founding cohort and on the yeast experiments; no allele-specific dominant-negative assay has been reported for p.Asn544Ser or p.Asp167Tyr, and p.Asp167Tyr lowered STT3A protein when expressed in cells, so the mechanism is established for the variant class rather than demonstrated for every allele.

evidence.snippet: STT3A encodes the catalytic subunit of the STT3A-containing oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex, essential for protein N-glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: Identifies STT3A as the catalytic subunit of OST-A. The sentence restates established biochemistry in the framing of a clinical paper, hence OTHER with a BACKGROUND quote role.

evidence.snippet: The OST subunit DC2 was placed at the interface between Sec61 and STT3A, where it acts as a versatile module for recruitment of STT3A-containing OST to the ribosome-Sec61 complex.
evidence.explanation: Structural evidence that the STT3A complex is the translocon-associated OST isoform.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical analysis showed that DC2 and KCP2 are responsible for mediating the interaction between the protein translocation channel and the STT3A complex.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the subunits that couple OST-A to the translocon.

steps/3.description: STT3A is the active-site subunit of OST-A, the oligosaccharyltransferase isoform recruited to the ribosome-Sec61 translocon through its DC2 and KCP2 subunits. It transfers the Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 oligosaccharide from its dolichol-pyrophosphate carrier onto asparagine in N-X-S/T sequons of nascent chains. Reduced or poisoned STT3A lowers the transfer activity of this complex. The lipid-linked donor is assembled normally, which distinguishes this lesion from the assembly-type CDG-I.

evidence.snippet: Mammals express two distinct OST complexes that act in a cotranslational (OST-A) or posttranslocational (OST-B) manner.
evidence.explanation: Defines OST-A as the cotranslational complex.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of site occupancy data disclosed several new classes of STT3A-dependent acceptor sites including those with suboptimal flanking sequences and sites located within cysteine-rich protein domains.
evidence.explanation: Identifies which acceptor sites depend on STT3A and so are lost when it fails.

evidence.snippet: the role of the STT3B complex in mediating cotranslational or posttranslocational glycosylation of acceptor sites that have been skipped by the STT3A complex
evidence.explanation: Review describing OST-B as the complex that picks up sites skipped by OST-A; evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

evidence.snippet: These distinct and complementary roles for the OST isoforms allow sequential scanning of polypeptides for acceptor sites to insure the maximal efficiency of N-glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: Explains why OST-B only partly compensates for OST-A loss.

evidence.snippet: We also show decreased glycosylation of STT3A-specific acceptors in fibroblasts from our patient
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of STT3A-dependent site occupancy in a recessive patient's fibroblasts.

steps/4.description: With OST-A impaired, acceptor sites are skipped as the nascent chain passes the translocon. STT3A-dependent sites include those with suboptimal flanking sequences and those inside cysteine-rich domains. OST-B can glycosylate some skipped sites afterwards, but the two complexes have complementary rather than redundant roles, so a subset of sites stays unoccupied. Patient fibroblasts show reduced glycosylation of STT3A-dependent acceptors.

evidence.snippet: The STT3A mutation significantly impairs glycosylation of the biomarker transferrin, but the STT3B mutation only slightly affects its glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: Shows hypoglycosylation of a circulating glycoprotein in the recessive form.

evidence.snippet: We present here a dominant form of STT3A-CDG that, because of the presence of abnormal transferrin glycoforms, is unusual among dominant type I CDGs.
evidence.explanation: Shows the same hypoglycosylation lesion in the dominant form.

steps/5.description: Glycoproteins leave the endoplasmic reticulum with unoccupied N-glycosylation sites. In serum this appears as transferrin molecules lacking whole glycans, the type I pattern, which is marked in the recessive form and ranges from classic to subtle in the dominant form.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies with STT3A-/- HEK293 cells showed severely reduced FVIII antigen and activity levels in conditioned media <10% expected, but normal intracellular levels.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the factor VIII defect to secretion in STT3A-null cells.

steps/6.description: Some STT3A-dependent N-glycans on coagulation factor VIII are needed for its efficient secretion. Cells lacking STT3A make normal intracellular amounts of factor VIII but release less than a tenth of the expected amount. In the reported patient the low plasma level was attributed to this secretion defect together with low von Willebrand factor.

evidence.snippet: We show reduced abundance of two canonical tyrosine receptor kinases - the insulin receptor and insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) - at the cell surface in STT3A-null cells, due to decreased N-linked glycan site occupancy and proteolytic processing in combination with increased endoplasmic reticulum localization.
evidence.explanation: Shows that STT3A loss impairs processing and surface delivery of two growth-factor receptors.

steps/7.description: In STT3A-null cells the insulin receptor and IGF-1 receptor reach the cell surface in reduced amounts, because their own N-glycan site occupancy is lower and because the proprotein convertase PCSK5a that cleaves them is itself underglycosylated. This is an established cell-line finding. Its relevance to patients is unshown: no study has measured these receptors in STT3A-CDG patient cells, and any contribution to the short stature of the dominant form is an inference (see discussions).

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, the increased expression of the ATF6 and PERK indicated that the unfolded protein response also happened in STT3A-KO cells.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence of unfolded protein response activation after STT3A deletion.

evidence.snippet: Remarkably, the lumenal ER chaperone GRP94 was hyperglycosylated in STT3A-deficient cells, bearing glycans on five silent sites in addition to the normal glycosylation site.
evidence.explanation: A marker change that the same study reproduces with ER-stress inducers.

steps/8.description: STT3A-knockout cells activate the unfolded protein response, with raised ATF6 and PERK, and the ER chaperone GRP94 becomes hyperglycosylated on normally silent sites, a change that ER-stress inducers reproduce in wild-type cells. This has been shown only in engineered cell lines; whether ER stress contributes to the patients' tissue phenotypes is untested.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous knockdown zebrafish exhibit phenotypes similar to those of patients, including craniofacial dysmorphology (increased eye distance, increased Basihyal's length, increased Ceratohyal's angle), skeletal abnormalities (reduced number of mineralized bones)
evidence.explanation: Reduced stt3a dosage alone produces skeletal and craniofacial defects in a vertebrate.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals presented with variable skeletal anomalies, short stature, macrocephaly, and dysmorphic features; half had intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: The human skeletal phenotype that this node accounts for.

steps/9.description: Skeletal involvement is the distinguishing feature of the dominant form. Heterozygous stt3a knockdown in zebrafish reduces the number of mineralized bones and alters craniofacial cartilage geometry, supporting a direct effect of reduced STT3A on skeletal development. Which STT3A-dependent glycoproteins mediate this is not known.

evidence.snippet: The two cases from unrelated consanguineous families both show neurologic abnormalities, hypotonia, intellectual disability, failure to thrive and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: The multisystem outflow in the recessive form.

evidence.snippet: Neurodevelopmental involvement was frequent, including motor delay (13/21), learning difficulties (13/21), speech delay (12/21), and intellectual disability (10/21).
evidence.explanation: The neurodevelopmental outflow in the dominant form.

steps/10.description: Underglycosylation of many client glycoproteins at once produces the neurodevelopmental, neuromuscular and systemic features. The recessive form is dominated by encephalopathy (developmental delay, intellectual disability, absent speech, seizures, hypotonia) and the dominant form by musculoskeletal and milder neurodevelopmental features. The dysmorphic, adipose, behavioral, hematologic and congenital-anomaly features of the dominant form are routed through this node as well, because the pooled cohort establishes them as features of the disease without naming a client glycoprotein for any of them. Which clients are rate-limiting for each feature has not been worked out, except for the coagulation factors.

evidence.snippet: Common phenotypic features in all symptomatic individuals include developmental delay, intellectual disability, with absent speech and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay in all symptomatic members of a recessive family.

evidence.snippet: STT3A-CDG (OMIM# 615596) is an autosomal recessive N-linked glycosylation disorder characterized by seizures, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and a type I carbohydrate deficient transferrin pattern.
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay is a defining feature of the recessive form.

steps/11.description: Present in every symptomatic individual with the recessive form. In the dominant form delay is usually confined to motor and speech milestones and is recorded under those phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Common phenotypic features in all symptomatic individuals include developmental delay, intellectual disability, with absent speech and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Intellectual disability in all symptomatic members of a recessive family.

evidence.snippet: Neurodevelopmental involvement was frequent, including motor delay (13/21), learning difficulties (13/21), speech delay (12/21), and intellectual disability (10/21).
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency in the dominant form.

steps/12.description: Present in all reported recessive cases and in about half of dominant cases (10 of 21 in the pooled dominant cohort), where it is usually milder.

evidence.snippet: Common phenotypic features in all symptomatic individuals include developmental delay, intellectual disability, with absent speech and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Absent speech in all symptomatic members of a recessive family.

evidence.snippet: Common phenotypic features in all symptomatic individuals include developmental delay, intellectual disability, with absent speech and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Seizures in all symptomatic members of a recessive family.

evidence.snippet: This report describes a 17-year-old male who was referred to the Undiagnosed Diseases Network (UDN) with a history of macrocephaly, failure to thrive, short stature, epilepsy, autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, mild developmental delay, intermittent hypotonia, dysmorphic features, and mildly enlarged aortic root.
evidence.explanation: Epilepsy in a patient with the dominant form.

steps/14.description: A core feature of the recessive form. Epilepsy has also been reported in the dominant form.

evidence.snippet: The two cases from unrelated consanguineous families both show neurologic abnormalities, hypotonia, intellectual disability, failure to thrive and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: Hypotonia in the index recessive patient.

evidence.snippet: This report describes a 17-year-old male who was referred to the Undiagnosed Diseases Network (UDN) with a history of macrocephaly, failure to thrive, short stature, epilepsy, autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, mild developmental delay, intermittent hypotonia, dysmorphic features, and mildly enlarged aortic root.
evidence.explanation: Intermittent hypotonia in a patient with the dominant form.

evidence.snippet: The two cases from unrelated consanguineous families both show neurologic abnormalities, hypotonia, intellectual disability, failure to thrive and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: Failure to thrive in the index recessive patient.

evidence.snippet: We describe a patient with a novel homozygous likely pathogenic missense variant c.1079A>C (p.Tyr360Ser) who presents with chronically low Factor VIII (FVIII) and von Willebrand Factor (vWF) levels and activities in addition to the previously reported symptoms of developmental delay and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Low factor VIII in the recessive form.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, the newly reported individuals expand dominant STT3A-CDG with previously unreported features, including anorectal malformation, morbid obesity, and clinically significant bleeding diathesis with von Willebrand factor and factor VIII deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Factor VIII deficiency in the dominant form.

steps/47.description: Chronically low factor VIII in one recessive patient homozygous for p.Tyr360Ser. In the dominant form coagulation factor deficiency was found in 5 of 21 individuals, and one had clinically significant bleeding with factor VIII and von Willebrand factor deficiency.
